# Two routes: Ephesians 2 and Romans 9


Two routes reach the conclusion, one through Ephesians 2 and one through
Romans 9, and each has a reading of its text that is in dispute. A third line,
from Romans 11:6, delivers only the first part of the conclusion, that
salvation is by grace, and every party walks it: Trent quotes the verse in the
eighth chapter of its decree on justification.

Trent and the Remonstrants each deny part of what the Reformed lines deliver,
so each has lines of its own here. Trent's fourth canon on justification denies
that the will is merely passive, and in the same sentence condemns anyone who
says the will cannot refuse its consent: so Trent's lines deny both the second
and third parts of the conclusion. The Remonstrants deny the second part, that
grace cannot be resisted, from Stephen's speech in Acts 7.

The texts of resistance are common ground. Stephen's hearers "always resist the
Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51), and Paul tells believers not to grieve the Spirit
(Ephesians 4:30) or quench him (1 Thessalonians 5:19); every party grants that
the Spirit's work meets resistance. What is disputed is the step from there to
the claim that the grace that saves can be *finally* refused. The word "resist"
can mean resisting for a time, as the Reformed say even the elect do before
grace overcomes them, or refusing to the end. A second route to the final
refusal runs through the sin that is never forgiven (Matthew 12:31–32), read
with Augustine as impenitence persisted in until death.

The closing step is two steps. From God's work alone to the will's passivity,
the Lutherans agree with Dort. From God's work alone to grace that cannot be
finally refused, they do not: the Formula of Concord holds conversion to be the
Spirit's work alone and grace resistible all the same.

## The positions, and the variants the results ask about


The rivals come first, because they were written first. Each is a position as
its own documents state it: Trent from the sixth session's decree and canons on
justification, the Remonstrants from their five articles of 1610 and from
Arminius. Neither is Pelagian. Both say, in so many words, that salvation is by
grace, and both packages carry the line from Romans 11:6 that delivers it.

Two more positions follow, each a way of holding grace and freedom together
that is neither Dort's nor the Remonstrants'. The Lutherans of the Formula of
Concord hold the will "purely passive" in conversion and grace resistible all
the same. Wesley holds that God restores to everyone a measure of the freedom
lost in Adam, so that each can receive the offer by faith or refuse it. And the
third way as it was put to this argument, that God gives the ability to believe
as Adam was made able to stand or fall, and faith alone receives, is stated
without saying which kind of help that ability is, because that is what a
dilemma below asks.

The variants after the Reformed package each change one thing, named, so that a
result about a variant is a result about that one change.

## What does and does not follow


The results come in three groups. The first is what each position reaches: the
Reformed premises reach sola gratia, neither rival's do, and both rivals reach
its first part. The second is which reading of the texts the Reformed case
depends on: neither alone, and the two together. The third is where Arminius
parts from the Ephesians strand, which is after the grammar of "this" and after
faith is granted to be God's gift.

### Satisfiability

A list of premises that contradict each other would "prove" anything, so each
position that reaches its conclusion is shown to be holdable without
contradiction, by Dort's reading. These are claims about the health of the
encoding, not about the dispute, and are not headline results.

#### The conclusion

<a id="solaGratia"></a>
**`solaGratia`**

**Sola gratia, stated sharply enough that the rivals divide from it.**
Salvation is by grace and not earned; the grace that saves brings about the
consent it seeks; and in being made alive the will contributes nothing. The
three parts are separate claims so that a rival can be shown holding the first
and denying one or both of the others: Trent's premises deny both, the
Remonstrants' the second.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}}\\)

</div>

#### The steps

<a id="graceStep"></a>
**`graceStep`**

Romans 11:6: if salvation is by grace it is not by works, so it is by grace
and not earned.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-4}{P_{4}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}}\\) — *would give:* Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act

</div>

<a id="ephesiansStep"></a>
**`ephesiansStep`**

Ephesians 2:8–9, with "this" read as pointing to the whole of being saved
by grace through faith: so faith, part of that whole, is God's gift. Rated
`disputed`: Robertson reads the pronoun the same way and calls the whole
"conditioned on faith on our part", and Calvin, on the next verse, writes "not
that faith is the gift of God, but that salvation is given to us by God".

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-17}{P_{17}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-19}{P_{19}}\\) — *would give:* Faith itself is God's gift

</div>

<a id="giftStep"></a>
**`giftStep`**

**The step Arminius refuses.** If faith is God's gift, and it is given to
those who were dead until God made them alive (Ephesians 2:1–5), then
conversion is God's work alone. Rated `disputed`: Arminius grants both grounds
and denies that the gift cannot be refused. Dort's answer is its article on
faith: God's gift "not on account of its being offered by God to man, to be
accepted or rejected at his pleasure, but because it is in reality conferred"
(III/IV, article 14).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-19}{P_{19}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-23}{P_{23}}\\) — *would give:* Conversion is God's work alone: God regenerates, and the will does nothing to it

</div>

<a id="romansStep"></a>
**`romansStep`**

Romans 9:16, read as being about salvation: if God's saving mercy "depends
not on human will or exertion", conversion is God's work alone. Rated
`disputed`: Arminius grants that the verse is about salvation and reads its
willing and running as seeking salvation by the works of the law, so that the
mercy goes to believers and can be refused.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-3}{P_{3}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-18}{P_{18}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-23}{P_{23}}\\) — *would give:* Conversion is God's work alone: God regenerates, and the will does nothing to it

</div>

<a id="passiveStep"></a>
**`passiveStep`**

From God's work alone to the third part of the conclusion: the will is
passive in being made alive. Rated `wellSupported`: the Lutherans, who part from
Dort on the next step, grant this one. It is taken as what Dort means by the
phrase: the new life is "a making alive, which God works in us without our aid"
(III/IV, article 12).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-23}{P_{23}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}}\\) — *would give:* In being made alive the will is passive, and contributes nothing to it

</div>

<a id="effectualStep"></a>
**`effectualStep`**

**From God's work alone to the second part of the conclusion: the grace that
saves cannot be finally refused.** Rated `disputed`: the Formula of Concord holds
conversion to be the Spirit's work alone, with the will "purely passive", and
holds grace resistible all the same.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-23}{P_{23}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}\\) — *would give:* The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks

</div>

<a id="textsOfResistanceStep"></a>
**`textsOfResistanceStep`**

What the texts of resistance say together: the Spirit's work is resisted.
Acts 7:51 says so of Stephen's hearers, and Paul's commands not to grieve the
Spirit (Ephesians 4:30) or quench him (1 Thessalonians 5:19) presuppose it of
believers.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}}\\) — *would give:* The Holy Spirit's work is resisted, by unbelievers and by believers

</div>

<a id="resistanceStep"></a>
**`resistanceStep`**

**From resistance to final refusal.** If the Spirit is resisted, and what is
resisted is the grace that saves, that grace can be finally refused. The
Remonstrants' fourth article, made explicit.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-20}{P_{20}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *would give:* The grace that saves can be finally refused

</div>

<a id="griefStep"></a>
**`griefStep`**

**From grieving the Spirit to final refusal.** If the Spirit is resisted,
and those who obstinately resist him can grieve and lose him, the grace that
saves can be finally refused. The Formula of Concord's reading of
Ephesians 4:30.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *would give:* The grace that saves can be finally refused

</div>

<a id="blasphemyStep"></a>
**`blasphemyStep`**

**From the unforgivable sin to final refusal.** If the blasphemy against the
Spirit is never forgiven (Matthew 12:31–32), and it is the final refusal of the
grace offered, then that grace can be finally refused.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-12}{P_{12}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *would give:* The grace that saves can be finally refused

</div>

<a id="refusalStep"></a>
**`refusalStep`**

What final refusal means for the second part of the conclusion: grace that
can be finally refused is not effectual of itself. Rated `consensus`: it is what
the two claims say, and their meanings exclude each other.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}\\) — *would deny:* The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks

</div>

<a id="cooperationStep"></a>
**`cooperationStep`**

**Trent's fourth canon, first half.** The will, moved by God, cooperates by
assenting, as "Return to me" calls on it to; so it is not passive. Rated
`disputed`: Aquinas grants that grace cooperates with a will that moves and
holds that in grace's first effect the mind "is moved and does not move".

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-21}{P_{21}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}}\\) — *would deny:* In being made alive the will is passive, and contributes nothing to it

</div>

<a id="dissentStep"></a>
**`dissentStep`**

**Trent's fourth canon, second half.** The will, moved by God, can refuse
if it wishes; so grace is not effectual of itself. Rated `disputed`: Aquinas
grants that a will God moves could, taken simply, fail to be moved, and still
holds that the man God moves to grace attains it infallibly.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{claims.html#claim-22}{P_{22}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}\\) — *would deny:* The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks

</div>

#### The rivals

<a id="tridentine"></a>
**`tridentine`** — Trent (Session VI, canon 4)

**Trent**, from the sixth session (1547). Romans 11:6, which its eighth
chapter quotes; Zechariah 1:3 read with Lamentations 5:21, as its fifth chapter
reads them; and canon 4, on the will that cooperates by assenting and can refuse
if it wishes.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

Grounded in scripture alone: Romans 11:6 — if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works.

<a id="remonstrant"></a>
**`remonstrant`** — Remonstrant (the Five Articles, 1610)

**The Remonstrants**, from their articles of 1610 and from Arminius.
Romans 11:6; the texts of resistance, which every party grants; the fourth
article, that grace is not irresistible, read from Acts 7:51; and what Arminius
grants of the Reformed case: the texts of Ephesians 2, that
faith is God's gift, and that Romans 9:16 is about salvation. What is left out
is the two steps from those to God's work alone, which are the steps he
refuses.

- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-20}{P_{20}}\\) — What Stephen's hearers resisted in Acts 7:51 was the grace that saves
- (6) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\) — Ephesians 2:1–5 — dead in trespasses, God made us alive together with Christ
- (7) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — Ephesians 2:8–9 — by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God
- (8) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-19}{P_{19}}\\) — Faith itself is God's gift

<a id="lutheran"></a>
**`lutheran`** — Lutheran (the Formula of Concord)

**The Lutherans**, from the Formula of Concord (1577) and the Augsburg
Confession (1530). Conversion is the Holy Spirit's work alone, and in it the
will is "purely passive"; yet those who obstinately resist the Spirit "grieve
and lose" him, so the grace that saves can be finally refused, and where it is,
the fault is the person's own. Grace is received by faith
alone.

- (6) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-23}{P_{23}}\\) — Conversion is God's work alone: God regenerates, and the will does nothing to it
- (7) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) — Grace is received by faith alone
- (8) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-4}{P_{4}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}}\\) — *would give:* Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act

<a id="wesleyan"></a>
**`wesleyan`** — Wesleyan (preventing grace)

grace that goes before ("preventing grace"), so that each is able to believe;
that grace can be resisted or yielded to; and it is received by faith alone.

<a id="thirdWay"></a>
**`thirdWay`** — The third way (an ability given, received by faith)

**The third way, as it was put to this argument.** As Adam was made able to
stand or to fall (Genesis 2:16–17), so God gives the one who hears the gospel
the ability to believe; the offer is real, and grace is received by faith alone.
Stated this way it does not say what kind of help the ability is, whether one
that makes believing possible or one that brings it about. It carries the step
every party grants, that grace which can be finally refused is not effectual of
itself, and nothing that would decide whether it can be.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-4}{P_{4}}\\) — Romans 11:6 — if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — Genesis 2:16–17 — of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) — God gives the ability to believe, as Adam was made able to stand or fall
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) — Grace is received by faith alone
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-4}{P_{4}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}}\\) — *would give:* Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act
- (6) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}\\) — *would deny:* The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) — *at issue:* \\(\href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}}\\) Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act; \\(\href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) Grace is received by faith alone

</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: Romans 11:6 — if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works, Genesis 2:16–17 — of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat.

<a id="objection"></a>
**`objection`** — The objection from the Spirit's resistance

**The objection from the Spirit's resistance, strengthened.** Three routes to
the claim that the grace that saves can be finally refused. Two run from the
texts of resistance: with the Remonstrants' reading of what Stephen's hearers
resisted, and with the Formula of Concord's reading of grieving the Spirit, that
it can end in losing him. The third runs from the sin that is never forgiven,
read with Augustine as impenitence to the end. It concludes the denial of the
second part of sola gratia, and nothing about the others.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}}\\) — Acts 7:51 — you always resist the Holy Spirit
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}}\\) — Ephesians 4:30 — do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}}\\) — 1 Thessalonians 5:19 — do not quench the Spirit
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-20}{P_{20}}\\) — What Stephen's hearers resisted in Acts 7:51 was the grace that saves
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}}\\) — Those who obstinately resist the Spirit can grieve and lose him
- (6) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}}\\) — Matthew 12:31–32 — the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven
- (7) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-12}{P_{12}}\\) — The blasphemy against the Spirit is impenitence to the end: grace refused till death
- (8) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}}\\) — *would give:* The Holy Spirit's work is resisted, by unbelievers and by believers
- (9) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-20}{P_{20}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *would give:* The grace that saves can be finally refused
- (10) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *would give:* The grace that saves can be finally refused
- (11) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-12}{P_{12}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *would give:* The grace that saves can be finally refused
- (12) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks

</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: Acts 7:51 — you always resist the Holy Spirit, Ephesians 4:30 — do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed, 1 Thessalonians 5:19 — do not quench the Spirit, Matthew 12:31–32 — the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.

#### The position argued for

the conclusion, and the Reformed answer to Acts 7:51.

#### The positions

<a id="reformed_establishes"></a>
**`reformed_establishes`**

**Grant the Reformed premises, and sola gratia follows.** The premises are
Romans 11:6; Ephesians 2, with "this" pointing to the whole of being saved by
grace through faith; Romans 9:16, read as being about salvation; the steps from
each of those to God's work alone; and the Reformed answer to Acts 7:51. The result
does not say that the readings or the steps are right, only that the conclusion
follows from them. Four of the steps are rated `disputed`, each on a reader who
grants its grounds and denies its conclusion: the step from "this" to faith as
a gift (Robertson), the steps from each strand to God's work alone (Arminius),
and the step from God's work alone to grace that cannot be finally refused (the
Formula of Concord).

```lean
theorem reformed_establishes : Establishes reformed
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="trentsReading"></a>
**`trentsReading`**

Trent's reading, written down: salvation is by grace, the will cooperates
and can refuse, so grace is not effectual of itself and the will is not passive
in being made alive, and grace is not received by faith alone (canon 9). Claims
Trent's documents do not address, such as the
readings of Ephesians 2 and Romans 9, are set true; nothing turns on them. On
these sixteen claims Trent's reading and Arminius's coincide; the two positions
differ in which premises they hold and whom they cite.

```lean
def trentsReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.faithAloneReceivesGrace => False
    | Claim.conversionIsGodsWorkAlone => False
    | Claim.graceIsEffectualOfItself => False
    | Claim.willIsPassiveInRegeneration => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="tridentine_not_establishes"></a>
**`tridentine_not_establishes`**

**Trent's premises do not lead to sola gratia.** A *countermodel* shows it: a
way of holding every one of Trent's premises while denying the conclusion. On
Trent's account the will,
moved by God, cooperates by assenting and can refuse its consent; so the second
and third parts of the conclusion fail. Whether canon 4 really denies the second
part is itself disputed, because Aquinas holds both that the will can refuse,
taken simply, and that the man God moves to grace attains it infallibly; that
dispute is in the rating of the canon's step, not in this result.

```lean
theorem tridentine_not_establishes : ¬Establishes tridentine
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="arminiusReading"></a>
**`arminiusReading`**

Arminius's reading, written down: salvation is by grace, faith is God's gift,
Romans 9:16 is about salvation, and the grace that saves can be refused. It also
sets the will's passivity false. The Remonstrants denied that too, but their
denial of it is not encoded, and nothing in their package turns on it. The
reading of "this" in Ephesians 2:8 is set true, as Hoehner and Robertson hold
it; no reading of the pronoun is cited to Arminius.

```lean
def arminiusReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.conversionIsGodsWorkAlone => False
    | Claim.graceIsEffectualOfItself => False
    | Claim.willIsPassiveInRegeneration => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="remonstrant_not_establishes"></a>
**`remonstrant_not_establishes`**

**The Remonstrants' premises do not lead to sola gratia either**, though they
grant much of what the Reformed case rests on: that faith is God's gift, given
to those dead in sin, and that Romans 9:16 is about salvation. What they add is
their fourth article, that grace is not irresistible, read from Acts 7:51; what
they leave out is the two steps from those grants to God's work alone.

```lean
theorem remonstrant_not_establishes : ¬Establishes remonstrant
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="rivals_hold_salvation_by_grace"></a>
**`rivals_hold_salvation_by_grace`**

Both rivals reach the first part, that salvation is by grace. Trent's premises
deliver it, and so do the Remonstrants', by the same line from Romans 11:6. A
conclusion stated only as "salvation is by grace" would be established by all
three positions and would divide none of them, which is why the conclusion here
has two further parts.

```lean
theorem rivals_hold_salvation_by_grace : Entails tridentine.premises (p
    Claim.salvationIsByGrace) ∧ Entails remonstrant.premises (p
    Claim.salvationIsByGrace)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="trent_denies_passivity"></a>
**`trent_denies_passivity`**

Trent's premises deny the third part, that the will is passive. Canon 4
condemns anyone who says the will "is merely passive", and the premises deliver
the denial outright. The step is rated `disputed`, because the canon speaks of
the will preparing itself for justification and the Reformed claim is about the
moment of being made alive.

```lean
theorem trent_denies_passivity : Entails tridentine.premises (notP
    Claim.willIsPassiveInRegeneration)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="trent_denies_effectual_grace"></a>
**`trent_denies_effectual_grace`**

Trent's premises deny the second part too, that grace is effectual of itself.
Canon 4 condemns anyone who says the will "cannot refuse its consent, if it
would", and the premises deliver the denial. The step is rated `disputed`:
Aquinas grants that the will moved by God could, taken simply, refuse, and
holds that the man God moves to grace "will infallibly attain to it". So a
Catholic reader in his school grants the canon and not this conclusion.

```lean
theorem trent_denies_effectual_grace : Entails tridentine.premises (notP
    Claim.graceIsEffectualOfItself)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="remonstrants_deny_effectual_grace"></a>
**`remonstrants_deny_effectual_grace`**

The Remonstrants' premises deny the second part: grace can be resisted. Their
fourth article reads Acts 7:51 so.

```lean
theorem remonstrants_deny_effectual_grace : Entails remonstrant.premises (notP
    Claim.graceIsEffectualOfItself)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Which reading the Reformed case depends on

<a id="touto_not_load_bearing"></a>
**`touto_not_load_bearing`**

The case does not depend on the reading of "this". Remove the reading on
which "this" in Ephesians 2:8 points to the whole of being saved by grace
through faith, keep everything else, and sola gratia still follows by
Romans 9:16, which does not use the Ephesians grammar. The reading itself is
well supported: Hoehner and Robertson both hold it.

```lean
theorem touto_not_load_bearing : Establishes reformedWithoutTouto
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="romans_reading_not_load_bearing"></a>
**`romans_reading_not_load_bearing`**

Nor does it depend on the reading of Romans 9:16. Remove the reading on which the verse
is about salvation, keep everything else, and sola gratia still follows by
Ephesians 2.

```lean
theorem romans_reading_not_load_bearing : Establishes
    reformedWithoutRomansReading
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="neitherReadingGranted"></a>
**`neitherReadingGranted`**

The reading on which neither of the two readings holds: "this" in
Ephesians 2:8 does not point to the whole, and Romans 9:16 is about God's choice
of a people for a part in history alone. No reader is cited who holds both
denials; the countermodel shows what follows if both readings go, not that
anyone has given them up. Everything else the Reformed position grants is kept,
the Reformed answer to Acts 7:51 included.

```lean
def neitherReadingGranted : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.toutoRefersToTheWhole => False
    | Claim.romans9_16ConcernsSalvation => False
    | Claim.faithIsGodsGift => False
    | Claim.conversionIsGodsWorkAlone => False
    | Claim.graceIsEffectualOfItself => False
    | Claim.willIsPassiveInRegeneration => False
    | Claim.acts7_51ResistsSavingGrace => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="readings_jointly_load_bearing"></a>
**`readings_jointly_load_bearing`**

The two readings together carry it. Remove both, keep every text and every
step, and sola gratia no longer follows, because nothing is left that reaches
God's work alone. So the Reformed case needs at least one of the two readings,
and either will do. A reading whose removal stops the conclusion following is
called *load-bearing*; here only the pair is.

```lean
theorem readings_jointly_load_bearing : ¬Establishes
    reformedWithoutEitherReading
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="ephesians_strand_establishes"></a>
**`ephesians_strand_establishes`**

The Ephesians strand, argued alone, reaches sola gratia. It rests on two
steps, both rated `disputed`: from "this" to faith as God's gift, and from the
gift to God's work alone.

```lean
theorem ephesians_strand_establishes : Establishes ephesiansStrand
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="romans_strand_establishes"></a>
**`romans_strand_establishes`**

So does the Romans strand, on one step rated `disputed`.

```lean
theorem romans_strand_establishes : Establishes romansStrand
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Where Arminius parts from the Ephesians strand

<a id="gift_of_faith_does_not_settle_resistibility"></a>
**`gift_of_faith_does_not_settle_resistibility`**

**That faith is God's gift does not settle whether grace can be refused.**
Grant everything the Ephesians strand rests on short of its last step: the
texts, "this" pointing to the whole, and so faith as God's gift, given to those
who were dead in sin. Leave out only the step from that gift to God's work
alone, and sola gratia does not follow.

Arminius grants the texts and that faith is God's gift; the reading of "this" is
Hoehner's and Robertson's, not cited to him. On a reading that grants all of
these, his, the conclusion fails. So where he parts from the strand is the step
from the gift to God's work alone. The encoding writes "faith is God's gift" as
one claim, and Dort and Arminius mean different things by it: for Dort a gift
"in reality conferred", for Arminius one that can be refused. The difference
shows here as Arminius refusing the step.

```lean
theorem gift_of_faith_does_not_settle_resistibility : ¬Establishes
    ephesiansWithoutTheGiftStep
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="dortReading"></a>
**`dortReading`**

Dort's reading: every claim of the Reformed position holds. What Stephen's
hearers resisted was the preached word, not the grace that saves; grieving the
Spirit does not end in losing him; the unforgivable sin is not the final refusal
of saving grace; and that grace cannot be finally refused.

```lean
def dortReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.acts7_51ResistsSavingGrace => False
    | Claim.savingGraceCanBeFinallyRefused => False
    | Claim.grievingCanLoseTheSpirit => False
    | Claim.blasphemyIsFinalRefusalOfGrace => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="reformed_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`reformed_is_satisfiable`**

The Reformed package has a model.

```lean
theorem reformed_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable reformed.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="reformedWithoutTouto_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`reformedWithoutTouto_is_satisfiable`**

The Reformed package without its reading of "this" has a model.

```lean
theorem reformedWithoutTouto_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    reformedWithoutTouto.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="reformedWithoutRomansReading_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`reformedWithoutRomansReading_is_satisfiable`**

The Reformed package without its reading of Romans 9:16 has a model.

```lean
theorem reformedWithoutRomansReading_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    reformedWithoutRomansReading.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="ephesiansStrand_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`ephesiansStrand_is_satisfiable`**

The Ephesians strand alone has a model.

```lean
theorem ephesiansStrand_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable ephesiansStrand.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="romansStrand_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`romansStrand_is_satisfiable`**

The Romans strand alone has a model.

```lean
theorem romansStrand_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable romansStrand.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```
